title: Design an Undo Mechanism
summary: The textbook Command-pattern application — model undo as a per-action inverse operation, not a full-state snapshot, backed by a history stack.

slides.markdown:
**Design an undo mechanism** — probably the cleanest real-world justification for the Command pattern you'll ever get asked to design live. The scoring signal is whether you reach for **an inverse operation per action**, not a full-state snapshot, as your default model.

A common weak answer treats undo as "save a copy of everything before each change" — it works, but doesn't scale and misses the point of the question. The strong answer: each action knows how to reverse itself.

The 10-minute bar: a `Command` interface with execute/undo, a history stack, and an answer for actions that don't cleanly invert.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying question: single-level undo, or a full undo/redo stack?
slides.markdown:
Ask whether the system needs **single-level undo** (undo the last action, that's it) or a **full undo/redo stack** (undo any number of steps back, then redo forward again). Single-level only needs to remember the one most recent command; a full stack needs an ordered history and a separate pointer for how far back you've undone.

Most real editors — text editors, design tools — need the full stack, so unless told otherwise, I'd design for it. A single-level answer is a strict subset worth mentioning as the simpler starting point.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: commands with inverses, a history stack
slides.markdown:
The shape: every user action becomes a **[Command](command-pattern)** object that knows both how to `execute()` itself and how to `undo()` itself — the inverse operation lives right next to the forward one, on the same object, so they can never drift out of sync.

A `CommandHistory` stack records executed commands in order. Undo pops the most recent command and calls its `undo()`. That's the entire mechanism — no global snapshotting, no diffing state before and after.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a Command interface and a CommandHistory stack
Follow-up: what about actions that can't be cleanly inverted, like sending an email?
slides.markdown:
Some actions have no true inverse — you can't un-send an email. I'd handle this one of two ways depending on the action. If there's a compensating action (send a follow-up "disregard previous email"), model `undo()` as that compensation rather than a literal reversal, and be explicit in the UI about what's happening.

If there's genuinely no reasonable undo — a payment has cleared, an email has left the building — the honest answer is to **not offer undo** for that action at all, or gate the original action behind a confirmation step instead, since undo can't help after the fact.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you support redo after an undo?
slides.markdown:
I'd keep two stacks instead of one: an **undo stack** (executed commands, most recent on top) and a **redo stack** (commands that were undone). `undo()` pops from the undo stack, calls `undo()`, and pushes the command onto the redo stack. `redo()` does the reverse — pop from redo, call `execute()` again, push back onto undo.

The subtlety: executing any **new** command after an undo must clear the redo stack. Otherwise a redo could reapply a command whose preconditions no longer hold, since the user has since taken a different path.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: does undo need to survive a process restart?
slides.markdown:
Ask this explicitly, since it changes what the history stack actually is. **In-memory-only** undo — the common case for most editors — just needs the `Command` objects to live in memory for the session; closing the app clears history, which users generally expect.

**Persistent undo** across restarts needs every command to be serializable — its parameters and its inverse logic reconstructable from disk — a meaningfully bigger ask, since `undo()` as a closure over live objects doesn't survive a restart the way a small serialized diff would.

slides.sectionTitle: Weak answer: storing full object snapshots for every action
slides.markdown:
**Weak answer:** before every action, deep-copy the entire relevant object graph and push the copy onto a stack; undo means restoring the copy.

**Why it's wrong:** this wastes memory proportional to object size times number of undoable actions, and it misses the actual design insight the question is testing — that most actions have a small, cheap inverse ("move back 10px") rather than needing a full snapshot restore.

**Correct model:** encode the inverse operation on the command itself; reserve full snapshots for the rare action that genuinely has no clean inverse.

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: re-running the entire history from scratch
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "To undo, I'll just replay every command from the start except the last one."

**Why it's wrong:** this is O(n) per undo instead of O(1), and it assumes every command is safely re-runnable from the same starting state — which breaks the moment any command has an external side effect, like sending a notification, that shouldn't fire again on replay.

**Correct model:** store per-command inverses and undo by calling them directly; never regenerate history by re-executing from scratch.

**Model** — each action is a `Command` with its own `execute()`/`undo()`, never a full snapshot. **History** — a stack of executed commands; undo pops and inverts. **Redo** — a second stack, cleared whenever a new command executes after an undo. **Non-invertible actions** — use a compensating action, or don't offer undo at all. **Close** by naming persistence: undo across a restart needs serializable commands, not just live closures.
